segments.text: - As designers, we're constantly giving
and receiving feedback.
It's the nature of our job.
While receiving feedback can be a lot to process,
so can giving helpful feedback.
For young designers, it can be hard to know
when to give feedback if what you're saying is helpful
or even having the confidence to provide feedback at all.
Here are three common issues and some tips
to help you build up your confidence
to provide visual feedback to others.
The first issue is not knowing how to structure feedback.
This can lead to one of two things,
providing unhelpful feedback or not saying anything at all.
We've all been there when someone has told us,
"I just don't like it," and thought to ourselves,
"Could you tell me why?"
To avoid being that critiquer,
my first tip is to think about your feedback
as a what, why, and how statement.
In other words, what element or action
are you wanting to give feedback for?
Why is it an issue related to the context of the design?
And if you have any suggestions,
how might they find a solution?
For example, the text you have
for the call to action link is too vague.
It might cause users to be confused
about what to expect after they click.
And if you have suggestions,
you can even add on by saying,
"You might be able to try this instead."
Now that you know how to structure feedback,
do you feel confident giving it?
It's common to be too shy to speak up,
to give your own thoughts about someone's work.
This could be because you feel like you
lack the necessary knowledge,
you don't wanna sound too critical or unintelligent,
or simply because you don't know how to phrase something.
My second tip is to remember you are there for a reason.
Just because you aren't a senior in the field
or maybe still in school,
doesn't mean you can't offer valuable feedback.
Being new to UX means you can offer a fresh perspective
that a seasoned professional might miss.
Or it might strike up thoughtful conversation
and be a learning experience for you.
The last common issue is not being comfortable
providing negative feedback.
While being able to emphasize the positives of a design
feels great for you and the designer,
it's the negative feedback that tends
to be the most valuable.
Constructive negative feedback leads to design improvements.
If all you are giving is positive feedback all the time,
it might mean you are uncomfortable bringing up concerns
you have during critique
because you think the designer might
take something the wrong way.
My last tip is to balance the positive
and negative feedback.
Bring up positive about a design
before bringing up the negative, or vice versa.
Just remember, any good designer will appreciate honest,
constructive, negative feedback.
To summarize, it's okay to be uncertain
about providing constructive feedback,
but in order to gain confidence, we have to practice.
Remember, remind yourself that your insights are valuable,
to structure your feedback, and balance the positives
and negatives during critique.
